Efficient Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search under Multi-Attribute Range Filter

Yuanhang Yu Affiliation: Tongji University, Shanghai, China email: yuanhangyu@tongji.edu.cn , Dawei Cheng Note: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Tongji University, Shanghai, China email: dcheng@tongji.edu.cn , Ying Zhang Affiliation: Zhejiang Gongshang University, Hangzhou, China email: ying.zhang@zjgsu.edu.cn , Lu Qin Affiliation: University of Technology Sydney, Sydney, Australia email: lu.qin@uts.edu.au , Wenjie Zhang Affiliation: The University of New South Wales, Sydney, Australia email: wenjie.zhang@unsw.edu.au and Xuemin Lin Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China email: xuemin.lin@sjtu.edu.cn
Abstract.

Nearest neighbor search on high-dimensional vectors is fundamental in modern AI and database systems. In many real-world applications, queries involve constraints on multiple numeric attributes, giving rise to range-filtering approximate nearest neighbor search (RFANNS). While there exist RFANNS indexes for single-attribute range predicates, extending them to the multi-attribute setting is nontrivial and often ineffective. In this paper, we propose KHI, an index for multi-attribute RFANNS that combines an attribute-space partitioning tree with HNSW graphs attached to tree nodes. A skew-aware splitting rule bounds the tree height by O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n), and queries are answered by routing through the tree and running greedy search on the HNSW graphs. Experiments on four real-world datasets show that KHI consistently achieves high query throughput while maintaining high recall. Compared with the state-of-the-art RFANNS baseline, KHI improves QPS by 2.46×2.46\times on average and up to 16.22×16.22\times on the hard dataset, with larger gains for smaller selectivity, larger kk, and higher predicate cardinality.

1. Introduction

Nearest neighbor search (NNS) is a fundamental problem in high-dimensional similarity search that has been extensively studied (Bentley, 1975; Indyk and Motwani, 1998; Li et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021b). Given a query object qq and a set OO of data objects in a metric space (S,δ)(S,\delta), nearest neighbor search aims to find an object o∗∈Oo^{*}\in O that minimizes δ⁡(q,o∗)\delta(q,o^{*}). Due to the curse of dimensionality (Indyk and Motwani, 1998), exact NNS is often impractical on large high-dimensional datasets, motivating extensive work on approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search (Malkov et al., 2014; Harwood and Drummond, 2016; Malkov and Yashunin, 2018; Fu et al., 2019; Jayaram Subramanya et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2025a). In modern systems, objects such as images, text, and videos are often represented as high-dimensional vectors. Consequently, ANN has become a fundamental operation in a wide range of applications, including information retrieval (Liu et al., 2007; Karpukhin et al., 2020), machine learning (Lewis et al., 2020; Guu et al., 2020), and vector database systems (Johnson et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021a).

Beyond vanilla ANN, there is increasing demand for ANN queries augmented with constraints on numeric attributes. This trend is evident both in recent research (Zuo et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024) and in industrial systems from Apple (Mohoney et al., 2023), Zilliz (Wang et al., 2021a), and Alibaba (Wei et al., 2020), where ANN queries are routinely combined with metadata filters on attributes such as time and popularity. In these setting, each data object consists of a feature vector together with a tuple of numeric attribute values, and queries are issued as a query vector accompanied by a range predicate over these attributes. For example, in a scholarly search engine, a user may submit a paper abstract as a query vector and retrieve similar publications whose publication year and citation count both fall within user-specified numeric ranges. In this paper, we study multi-attribute range-filtering approximate nearest neighbor search (RFANNS) in Euclidean space.

Existing RFANNS indexes (Zuo et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024) are primarily tailored to single-attribute range predicates. The multi-attribute setting is more challenging and is not handled effectively by existing RFANNS indexes. Specifically, the method in (Zuo et al., 2024) does not admit a straightforward extension to multiple attributes, while the index proposed in (Xu et al., 2024) explicitly supports multi-attribute range predicates but suffers from efficiency limitations in this regime. To address this challenge, one natural approach is to first partition the low-dimensional attribute space and then build graph indexes over the objects associated with each partition. R-trees are a well-established choice for the partitioning structure, as they are widely used for multidimensional spatial indexing. However, we argue that the substantial overlap among R-tree nodes degrades the quality of the graph indexes constructed over these partitions.

Motivated by these limitations, we propose KHI, an RFANNS index tailored for multi-attribute numeric range predicates. Specifically, KHI combines a KD-tree–like partitioning tree TT over the attribute space with graph indexes attached to its nodes. The partitioning tree recursively splits the data along individual attribute dimensions, producing non-overlapping partitions that adapt to attribute distributions. To keep the tree height under control in the presence of skewed attributes, we adopt a skew-aware splitting rule that only accepts reasonably balanced splits, guided by a balance threshold τ\tau and a small per-node exclusion set of problematic dimensions. We show that this rule guarantees an O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) bound on the tree height, where nn is the number of data objects. On top of this tree, each node p∈Tp\in T stores a single-level HNSW graph GpG_{p} built on the object subset 𝒪⁡(p)\mathcal{O}(p) covered by its partition.

To answer RFANNS queries efficiently, KHI leverages both the partitioning tree and the HNSW graphs. Given a query Q=(q,B)Q=(q,B), where qq is the query vector and BB is a range predicate that constrains the attribute values, we first traverse the tree to identify nodes whose attribute-space partitions intersect BB and select a small subset of them as entry points. Starting from these entry points, the algorithm performs a greedy search. When a candidate object is expanded, we reconstruct its neighborhood by aggregating incident edges from all HNSW graphs containing that object and retain only in-range neighbors whose attribute tuples satisfy BB. Together, these components enable efficient retrieval of the kk nearest neighbors satisfying the range predicate BB.

To construct KHI, we first build the partitioning tree TT in the attribute space using the skew-aware splitting strategy. Given TT, we then generate single-level HNSW graphs for all tree nodes in a bottom-up fashion: at each leaf node pp, we build the graph GpG_{p} directly over its object set 𝒪⁡(p)\mathcal{O}(p), and at internal nodes we reuse and incrementally merge the child graphs instead of rebuilding them from scratch. To further reduce index construction time, we employ a hybrid parallelization strategy that combines level-wise parallelism across tree nodes with intra-node parallelism during graph merging within individual tree nodes.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows.

  • •

    To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that specifically studies RFANNS with multi-attribute numeric range predicates in Euclidean space.

  • •

    We propose KHI, a new RFANNS index that combines an attribute-space partitioning tree with HNSW graphs anchored at tree nodes, and design an efficient RFANNS query algorithm that uses only in-range neighbors while still achieving high recall and high query throughput (Section 4).

  • •

    We conduct an extensive experimental study on four real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that at recall 0.950.95 (or 0.90.9), KHI improves QPS over a state-of-the-art RFANNS baseline by an average of 2.46×2.46\times, and up to 16.22×16.22\times on the hard dataset. (Section 5).

In addition, Section 2 presents the problem definition and basic background, Section 6 provides a detailed discussion of related work, and Section 7 concludes the paper.

2. Preliminaries

2.1. Problem Definition

Let SS be the dd-dimensional space and δ\delta: S×S→ℝS\times S\to\mathbb{R} be the distance function over SS. The kk-nearest neighbor (kk-NN) search problem with numerous real-world applications is defined as follows:

Definition 0.

(kk-NN). Given a finite set X⊆SX\subseteq S, a query vector q∈Sq\in S, a distance function δ\delta over SS, and a positive integer k≤nk\leq n, the kk-nearest neighbor search returns a subset R⊆XR\subseteq X with |R|=k|R|=k such that ∀x∈R\forall x\in R, ∀y∈X∖R\forall y\in X\setminus R: δ⁡(x,q)≤δ⁡(y,q)\delta(x,q)\leq\delta(y,q).

In practice, kk–NN search is often performed over vectors whose dimensionality ranges from tens to hundreds. A notable example is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Lewis et al., 2020). As dimensionality increases, the curse of dimensionality (Indyk and Motwani, 1998) renders exact nearest neighbor search computationally prohibitive. Therefore, approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search has attracted significant interest for achieving high efficiency at the cost of only a slight loss in accuracy. This loss is commonly quantified by the recall metric: given a set R^\hat{R} of size kk returned by an ANN algorithm, recall is defined as |R∩R^|/k|R\cap\hat{R}|/k, where RR denotes the true kk nearest neighbors.

In real-world applications, objects represented as vectors are often associated with structured attributes. For example, each product on e-commerce platforms can be represented by an image embedding and structured attributes (e.g., price and rating). Unless otherwise stated, we use vector and embedding interchangeably for the high-dimensional representation of an object. In this setting, one may desire to retrieve products that are similar in the embedding space while satisfying attribute filters, such as a given price range and a rating above 44. This type of search is known as the range-filtering nearest neighbor search (RFNNS). To formally define RFNNS, we first present a schema-style description of the object set, analogous to a relation schema in relational databases.

Definition 0.

(Object Schema). An object schema is defined as a pair (S,A)(S,A), where (1) S⊆ℝdS\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} denotes the embedding space; (2) A=(a1,…,am)A=(a_{1},\dots,a_{m}) specifies the attribute schema, where each aia_{i} is a numeric attribute.

Given an object schema (S,A)(S,A), an object oo under this schema is represented as a pair (x,t)(x,t), where x∈Sx\in S is a dd-dimensional vector and t=(t1,…,tm)t=(t_{1},\dots,t_{m}) is a tuple attribute values conforming to AA. An object set OO is an instance of (S,A)(S,A) if every o∈Oo\in O follows this representation. Now, we formally define RFNNS as follows:

Definition 0.

(RFNNS). Given an object schema (S,A)(S,A), its instance OO, a distance function δ\delta over SS, and a positive integer kk, an RFNNS query is defined as Q=(q,B)Q=(q,B), where q∈Sq\in S is a query vector and BB is a range predicate. Specifically, B={bi=[li,ri]∣i∈𝒥}B=\{b_{i}=[l_{i},r_{i}]\mid i\in\mathcal{J}\} where ∅≠𝒥⊆{1,…,m}\emptyset\neq\mathcal{J}\subseteq\{1,\dots,m\} specifies a non-empty set of constrained attributes. An object oo satisfies BB, denoted as o⊧Bo\models B, if li≤o.t.ti≤ri,∀i∈𝒥l_{i}\leq o.t.t_{i}\leq r_{i},\forall i\in\mathcal{J}. Let OB={o∈O∣o⊧B}O_{B}=\{o\in O\mid o\models B\} denote the filtered object set of OO under BB. The RFNNS problem is to find a set RQ⊆OBR_{Q}\subseteq O_{B} with |RQ|=k|R_{Q}|=k such that for any ox=(x,tx)∈RQo_{x}=(x,t_{x})\in R_{Q} and oy=(y,ty)∈OB∖RQo_{y}=(y,t_{y})\in O_{B}\setminus R_{Q}, δ⁡(x,q)≤δ⁡(y,q)\delta(x,q)\leq\delta(y,q).

We refer to |B|=|𝒥||B|=|\mathcal{J}| as the cardinality of BB, i.e., the number of constrained attributes. To illustrate the above definitions, we consider Example 4.

Example 0.

Given an object schema (S,A)(S,A) with m=2m=2, its instance O={oi∣i∈[1,8]}O=\{o_{i}\mid i\in[1,8]\} is presented in Figure 1. Consider an RFNNS query Q=(q,B)Q=(q,B) with k=2k=2, where qq and B={b1=[3.0,4.0],b2=[4.0,6.0]}B=\{b_{1}=[3.0,4.0],b_{2}=[4.0,6.0]\} are illustrated in Figure 1(a) and Figure 1(b), respectively. OB={o3,o4,o5,o6}O_{B}=\{o_{3},o_{4},o_{5},o_{6}\} based on their attribute tuples in Figure 1(b). For example, o3⊧Bo_{3}\models B because 3.0≤o3.t.t1≤4.03.0\leq o_{3}.t.t_{1}\leq 4.0 and 4.0≤o3.t.t2≤6.04.0\leq o_{3}.t.t_{2}\leq 6.0. As depicted in Figure 1(a), since the vectors of objects o3o_{3} and o4o_{4} are closer to qq than that of o5o_{5} and o6o_{6}, RQ={o3,o4}R_{Q}=\{o_{3},o_{4}\} is returned for the query QQ.

Since RFNNS faces challenges analogous to exact kk-NN, i.e., high computational cost at scale, we focus on the approximate variant of RFNNS, referred to as RFANNS, and throughout this paper we use the Euclidean distance as the distance function δ\delta.

2.2. Graph-based ANN Solutions

We briefly review graph-based ANN methods, which are adopted as core modules of RFANNS methods due to their ability to achieve high recall while probing only a small fraction of the dataset.

Graph-based methods construct a proximity graph GG where each vertex uu corresponds to a data vector in the dataset. Given a query vector qq, they perform a greedy graph traversal, starting from an entry point and iteratively moving to neighbors that are closer to qq until no closer candidate can be found. In practice, the search quality is controlled by a parameter ef, which limits the size of closest elements maintained during search. A larger ef typically explores more vertices, thus improving recall at the cost of higher query time. Note that ef is independent of kk: kk defines the query result size, while ef controls the search breadth. Existing graph-based methods (Malkov et al., 2014; Harwood and Drummond, 2016; Malkov and Yashunin, 2018; Li et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2019) primarily differ in their graph construction strategies, which in turn affect the efficiency and effectiveness of greedy navigation. Among them, NSW (Malkov et al., 2014) and HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, 2018) have been widely adopted, as they offer an excellent trade-off between search accuracy and efficiency at scale and often exhibit near-logarithmic search path length in practice.

Navigable small world graphs. NSW builds the proximity graph GG by inserting vertices corresponding to data vectors in sequence. For each inserted vertex uu, it performs a greedy search on the current graph to obtain an approximate neighbor set R^\hat{R} of size MM, and then adds symmetric edges between uu and each v∈R^v\in\hat{R}. Here, the parameter MM specifies the number of neighbors linked for each inserted vertex, thus controlling the graph density. Similarly, the result quality of construction-time search is controlled by the parameter efb\textit{ef}_{b}, which bounds the size of the candidate set explored during insertion. After inserting all vertices, the construction terminates. This incremental strategy yields a mix of two critical link types: short-range links that approximate local Delaunay neighborhoods (Aurenhammer, 1991) to facilitate fine-grained local exploration around the query vector, and long-range links formed during early insertions to enable fast navigation from distant regions toward the vicinity of the query vector, which together promote small-world navigability and lead to strong empirical efficiency.

Hierarchical navigable small world graphs. Building upon incremental construction of NSW, HNSW further introduces a hierarchical structure to improve scalability. Inspired by skip lists, HNSW organizes the proximity graph into multiple layers, where each layer is an NSW-like graph. The expected number of vertices increases exponentially from the top layer to the bottom layer, enabling a coarse-to-fine greedy traversal. To reduce redundant connections, HNSW adopts a heuristic neighbor selection strategy inspired by the Relative Neighborhood Graph (RNG) (Toussaint, 1980). Specifically, an edge (u,v)(u,v) is retained only if there exists no neighbor v′v^{\prime} of uu such that δ⁡(u,v′)<δ⁡(u,v)\delta(u,v^{\prime})<\delta(u,v) and δ⁡(v,v′)<δ⁡(u,v)\delta(v,v^{\prime})<\delta(u,v); this prunes edges that are shielded by closer intermediate neighbors. This strategy keeps the graph sparse while ensuring diverse directional connectivity, which is crucial for efficient greedy routing. To control graph density, HNSW bounds the maximum degree of each vertex, using MM for the upper layers and 2​M2M for the bottom layer.

2.3. Existing RFANNS Solutions

Existing RFANNS solutions (Zuo et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024) primarily focus on the single-attribute setting, i.e., m=1m=1, where the range predicate BB reduces to a query range [l,r][l,r]. In this setting, these methods follow an intuitive paradigm that supports efficient search over the filtered object set OBO_{B} under an arbitrary BB. Specifically, motivated by the strong empirical performance of HNSW, they seek to enable greedy search over OBO_{B} as if an HNSW graph were built on the vectors in OBO_{B}. We denote this HNSW graph as Gh​(OB)G_{h}(O_{B}) and refer to any HNSW graph built on a subset of OO as a filtered HNSW graph. Since constructing a filtered HNSW graph for every possible query range is prohibitive in both space and build time, these methods typically (i) locate an entry point within OBO_{B}, and (ii) recover, exactly or approximately, the neighbor list of each visited vertex uu on the fly, matching the neighbors that uu would have in Gh​(OB)G_{h}(O_{B}). Similarly, each vertex in the graph corresponds to an object in OO. Let OO be the object set with |O|=n|O|=n. Without loss of generality, we assume that its one-dimensional attribute domain is discretized and normalized to the integer range [0,n−1][0,n{-}1].

SeRF (Zuo et al., 2024). The discretized attribute domain yields O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) possible query ranges. SeRF aims to losslessly compress the filtered HNSW graphs associated with these O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) query ranges, thereby enabling exact on-the-fly reconstruction of the neighbor list for any visited vertex. This is achieved by compressing neighbor lists across adjacent ranges with the same left boundary.

For a fixed left boundary ll, as the right boundary rr increases from ll to n−1n{-}1, the membership of a vertex vv in the neighbor list of another vertex uu is non-reentrant, i.e., vv enters and eventually exits without reappearing. This behavior enables compact encoding via an inner interval [ts,te][t_{s},t_{e}], such that vv is a neighbor of uu for all ranges [l,r][l,r] with r∈[ts,te]r\in[t_{s},t_{e}]. Moreover, an outer interval [tl,tr][t_{l},t_{r}] specifies the range of left boundaries ll for which the inner interval [ts,te][t_{s},t_{e}] remains valid. That is, for any l∈[tl,tr]l\in[t_{l},t_{r}], vv is a neighbor of uu in all query ranges [l,r][l,r] where r∈[ts,te]r\in[t_{s},t_{e}].

During query processing, SeRF leverages these intervals to exactly recover, on the fly, the neighbor list of each visited vertex for an arbitrary query range B=[l,r]B=[l,r], while an entry point in OBO_{B} can be efficiently located by ordering objects according to their attribute values.

iRangeGraph (Xu et al., 2024). iRangeGraph supports approximate, rather than exact, on-the-fly neighbor reconstruction. To this end, iRangeGraph constructs HNSW graphs over a moderate number of ranges, achieving provable bounds on index space and construction time. Let us refer to a neighbor vv of a vertex uu as an in-range neighbor with respect to BB if v⊧Bv\models B; otherwise, vv is an out-of-range neighbor.

iRangeGraph organizes the attribute domain into subranges using a segment tree with O⁡(n)O(n) nodes, where each node corresponds to a subrange of [0,n−1][0,n{-}1]. For each subrange, the corresponding filtered HNSW graph is built. Given a query range [l,r][l,r], iRangeGraph reconstructs the neighbor list of each visited vertex uu by aggregating its neighbors from the filtered HNSW graphs associated with the segment-tree nodes containing uu, and retaining only in-range neighbors. An entry point in OBO_{B} can be efficiently obtained from the segment-tree nodes covered by [l,r][l,r].

To extend its single-attribute index to multiple attributes, iRangeGraph introduces a probabilistic neighbor-reconstruction rule that retains out-of-range neighbors from each filtered HNSW graph with a decaying probability. This relaxation enlarges the search space and thus improves result quality under multi-attribute range predicates, although the index is built on a single attribute.

3. Motivation

3.1. Limitations of Existing RFANNS Solutions

Existing RFANNS methods have demonstrated strong performance in the single-attribute setting. However, their extensions to multiple attributes are either impractical or ineffective. We detail these limitations below.

Limitations of SeRF. SeRF achieves strong performance in the single-attribute setting by enabling exact on-the-fly neighbor reconstruction for each visited vertex. However, this idea does not scale straightforwardly to multiple attributes. As the number of attributes in AA increases, the space of possible range predicates BB can grow exponentially, which would lead to prohibitive index construction time and space overhead. Therefore, SeRF becomes impractical in the multi-attribute setting.

Limitations of iRangeGraph. iRangeGraph supports the multi-attribute setting through a probabilistic rule that allows the search to access out-of-range neighbors with a decaying probability. This strategy lies between in-filtering and post-filtering: it relaxes the strict in-range constraint of in-filtering, while remaining more selective than post-filtering in exploring all out-of-range neighbors.

However, this relaxation also causes iRangeGraph to inherit a key drawback of post-filtering. For practical multi-attribute RFANNS queries where a subset of attributes are constrained, the filtered set OBO_{B} is often sparse in OO, i.e., the selectivity σ=|OB|/|O|\sigma=|O_{B}|/|O| is low, so the neighbor lists reconstructed on the fly by iRangeGraph contain only a small fraction of in-range neighbors. As a result, the search traverses many out-of-range objects, which slows the refinement of the best-so-far candidates and can even cause the number of visited objects to exceed |OB||O_{B}| when σ\sigma is sufficiently low. Our experiments in Section 4.2 confirm that this makes iRangeGraph less effective for multi-attribute RFANNS queries, despite its practical utility as an extension of a single-attribute index.

Implications. The above discussion shows that the multi-attribute setting poses two intertwined challenges that existing RFANNS methods do not sufficiently address. First, the space of possible range predicates grows rapidly with the number of attributes, making exact on-the-fly neighbor reconstruction for arbitrary BB unsustainable. This suggests approximating the neighbor lists in Gh​(OB)G_{h}(O_{B}) using only a moderate number of selectively constructed filtered HNSW graphs. Second, when the selectivity σ\sigma is relatively low, out-of-range expansions tend to dominate the search cost. Thus, an effective index should preserve strong search quality even when traversal is restricted to in-range neighbors.

These observations motivate the following design. We treat the tuples of objects in OO as points in the attribute space and organize them with a spatial partitioning structure. This structure induces a collection of subsets of OO, and on each subset we build a corresponding filtered HNSW graph. By maintaining a moderate number of such graphs, we aim to obtain a close approximate to, for an arbitrary multi-attribute range predicate BB, the HNSW graph Gh​(OB)G_{h}(O_{B}) and thereby achieve a practical balance between query performance and index cost.

3.2. Limitations of R-tree

Given the above implications, our next step is to identify a spatial index that can partition the attribute space into subsets. The R-tree is a natural candidate, as it is a classic index for organizing multi-dimensional points and supporting range queries. We thus examine whether an R-tree over the tuples can induce partitions that are well aligned with our partition-driven graph construction. As we show next, however, R-tree partitions do not consistently satisfy this requirement. To avoid confusion, we use node for tree structures and vertex for graph structures.

Overlapping MBRs. In an R-tree, each internal node stores the minimum bounding rectangles (MBRs) of its children, and the MBRs stored in the same internal node are allowed to overlap in order to maintain balance and compact bounding rectangles. Thus, the portion of the attribute space indexed by an internal node is represented by overlapping MBRs rather than disjoint cells, and two objects that are close in the attribute space can be assigned to different child nodes of the same parent.

Neighbor quality issues. In general, distances in the attribute space and in the embedding space are not necessarily aligned: objects that are far apart in the attribute space may still be close in the embedding space, and vice versa. Since sibling MBRs in an internal R-tree node are allowed to overlap, consider a case where two objects that are close in the attribute space, say ouo_{u} and ovo_{v}, fall into different child nodes p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} of the same parent p0p_{0}, while another object owo_{w} that is farther from ouo_{u} in the attribute space falls into the same node p1p_{1} as ouo_{u}. At the same time, owo_{w} may be much closer to ouo_{u} than ovo_{v} in the embedding space.

Let 𝒪⁡(p)\mathcal{O}(p) be the set of objects whose tuples fall within the MBR of the tree node pp. For brevity, we write Gp=Gh​(𝒪⁡(p))G_{p}=G_{h}(\mathcal{O}(p)). When we build Gp1G_{p_{1}}, the neighbors of ouo_{u} are restricted to the objects in 𝒪⁡(p1)\mathcal{O}(p_{1}). Since owo_{w} is among the closest objects to ouo_{u} in the embedding space within 𝒪⁡(p1)\mathcal{O}(p_{1}), owo_{w} becomes a neighbor of ouo_{u}. When Gp0G_{p_{0}} is constructed, owo_{w}, which is close to ouo_{u} in the embedding space, tends to remain in one of the neighbor slots of ouo_{u}. In contrast, ovo_{v}, which resides in the different child node p2p_{2}, is pruned due to the limited neighbor-list capacity of ouo_{u} and will no longer be considered as a neighbor of ouo_{u} in subsequent graph construction. As a result, the index systematically misses attribute-close neighbors of ouo_{u}, such as ovo_{v}, degrading the quality of the local neighborhood around objects. For a given range predicate BB, queries may either fail to retrieve certain relevant objects in OBO_{B} or reach them only via longer paths, thereby increasing search cost.

Example 0.

Given the object set OO shown in Figure 1, an example R-tree built over OO is depicted in Figure 2(a). Since sibling MBRs in the R-tree may overlap, the closest pair of objects in the attribute space, o3o_{3} and o4o_{4}, is assigned to two different leaf nodes, p4p_{4} and p5p_{5}. We focus on o4o_{4} and its neighbor lists across the R-tree levels.

As shown in Figure 2(b), at node p5p_{5} we have 𝒪⁡(p5)={o4,o5}\mathcal{O}(p_{5})=\{o_{4},o_{5}\}, and the neighbor list of o4o_{4} is {o5}\{o_{5}\}. At its parent p2p_{2}, additional objects such as o7o_{7} and o8o_{8} are present; because o7o_{7} and o5o_{5} are closer to o4o_{4} than o8o_{8} in the embedding space, the neighbor list of o4o_{4} becomes {o7,o5}\{o_{7},o_{5}\}. At the root p0p_{0}, more objects including o2o_{2} are considered, and the neighbor list of o4o_{4} is updated to {o2,o7}\{o_{2},o_{7}\}. Note that o3o_{3} and o4o_{4} first co-occur in the same object set only at p0p_{0}, i.e., o3,o4∈𝒪⁡(p0)o_{3},o_{4}\in\mathcal{O}(p_{0}). However, by that time the two neighbor slots of o4o_{4} are already occupied by o2o_{2} and o7o_{7}, which are farther from o4o_{4} than o3o_{3} in the attribute space. Consequently, the attribute-close neighbor o3o_{3} is excluded from the neighbor list of o4o_{4} at all levels. For a range predicate BB such that o3,o4∈OBo_{3},o_{4}\in O_{B}, a graph-based search that starts from o4o_{4} and expands along its neighbors may therefore fail to retrieve o3o_{3}, even though o3o_{3} is the closest attribute neighbor of o4o_{4}.

Implications. These observations indicate that overlapping partitions in the attribute space distort the neighborhood structure of filtered HNSW graphs and harm search quality (see (Yu et al., 2025) for details). Thus, for RFANNS, spatial indexes that induce non-overlapping partitions in the attribute space are therefore preferable.

4. Our Solution

4.1. Index Overview

We propose a KD-tree–HNSW hybrid index, denoted by KHI, which integrates a KD-tree–like partitioning tree on attribute tuples with filtered HNSW graphs over vectors.

Attribute-space partitioning. KHI maintains a binary partitioning tree TT on the attribute tuples of OO. Each node pp in TT is associated with (1) an axis-aligned hyper-rectangle ℛ⁡(p)\mathcal{R}(p) in the mm-dimensional attribute space, and (2) an object subset 𝒪⁡(p)⊆O\mathcal{O}(p)\subseteq O, defined as 𝒪(p)={o∈O∣o.t∈ℛ(p)}\mathcal{O}(p)=\{o\in O\mid o.t\in\mathcal{R}(p)\}. For the root node prp_{r}, ℛ⁡(pr)\mathcal{R}(p_{r}) covers all attribute tuples and 𝒪⁡(pr)=O\mathcal{O}(p_{r})=O. A node pp is a leaf if |𝒪⁡(p)|≤cl|\mathcal{O}(p)|\leq c_{l}, where clc_{l} is the leaf-capacity parameter (set to 22 in our implementation).

When splitting an internal node pp, KHI proceeds as follows. KHI first chooses a splitting dimension 𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p)∈{1,…,m}{\mathsf{Dim}}(p)\in\{1,\dots,m\} and a split value s⁡(p)s(p). Along dimension 𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p){\mathsf{Dim}}(p), we split the region ℛ⁡(p)\mathcal{R}(p) at s⁡(p)s(p) into two disjoint child regions ℛ⁡(pℓ)\mathcal{R}(p_{\ell}) and ℛ⁡(pr)\mathcal{R}(p_{r}). Objects with o.t.t𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p)≤s⁡(p)o.t.t_{{\mathsf{Dim}}(p)}\leq s(p) are assigned to the left child, and those with o.t.t𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p)>s⁡(p)o.t.t_{{\mathsf{Dim}}(p)}>s(p) to the right. To keep the tree reasonably balanced, we follow a round-robin rule for choosing the splitting dimension: 𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p){\mathsf{Dim}}(p) is set to the next dimension after the splitting dimension of its parent node (wrapping around after mm). Given 𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p){\mathsf{Dim}}(p), we collect the values {o.t.t𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p)∣o∈𝒪(p)}\{o.t.t_{{\mathsf{Dim}}(p)}\mid o\in\mathcal{O}(p)\} and set s⁡(p)s(p) to their median. However, this median-based choice of s⁡(p)s(p) may still lead to a highly unbalanced partition on skewed data. To mitigate this, we enforce a balance threshold τ>1\tau>1. Let nLn_{L} and nRn_{R} denote the numbers of objects assigned to the left and right child of pp, respectively. If max⁡{nL,nR}min⁡{nL,nR}≥τ\frac{\max\{n_{L},n_{R}\}}{\min\{n_{L},n_{R}\}}\geq\tau, we regard dimension 𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p){\mathsf{Dim}}(p) as skewed at pp, , exclude this dimension from consideration, and retry the split using the next available dimension. Once excluded at pp, a dimension is no longer used as a splitting dimension for any descendant of pp.

Lemma 0.

The height of TT is O⁡(log⁡ncl)O(\log\frac{n}{c_{l}}).

Proof sketch. Let N=|𝒪⁡(p)|N=|\mathcal{O}(p)| for an internal node pp, and assume nL≥nRn_{L}\geq n_{R}. From nLnR<τ\frac{n_{L}}{n_{R}}<\tau and nL+nR=Nn_{L}+n_{R}=N, we obtain nL<ττ+1​Nn_{L}<\frac{\tau}{\tau+1}N. Hence, after each recursive split, the larger child has size at most ρ​N\rho N, where ρ=ττ+1<1\rho=\frac{\tau}{\tau+1}<1. Starting from nn objects at the root, the size of any node is at most ρh​n\rho^{h}n after hh levels. The recursion stops once |𝒪⁡(p)|≤cl|\mathcal{O}(p)|\leq c_{l}, which implies ρh​n≤cl\rho^{h}n\leq c_{l} and therefore h≤log1/ρ⁡ncl=O⁡(log⁡ncl)h\leq\log_{1/\rho}\frac{n}{c_{l}}=O(\log\frac{n}{c_{l}}). □\square

Embedding-space graphs. For each node pp in TT, KHI builds a filtered HNSW graph GpG_{p}. The vertex set of GpG_{p} consists of the objects in 𝒪⁡(p)\mathcal{O}(p), and edges are constructed by the standard HNSW procedure. In our implementation, each GpG_{p} is a single-level HNSW graph (L=1L=1): the KD-tree–like hierarchy already provides the coarse-to-fine search structure, so additional HNSW layers are unnecessary. We use MM to bound the maximum degree of each vertex in all single-level HNSW graphs.

Example 0.

Consider the object set OO in Figure 1 and the leaf capacity is cl=2c_{l}=2. The partitioning tree TT of KHI on OO is illustrated in Figure 3(a). At the root p0p_{0}, KHI splits on the first attribute, i.e., 𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p0)=1{\mathsf{Dim}}(p_{0})=1, with split value s⁡(p0)=3.4s(p_{0})=3.4, the median of the first-attribute values in 𝒪⁡(p0)\mathcal{O}(p_{0}). Objects with o.t.t1≤3.4o.t.t_{1}\leq 3.4 are assigned to the left child p1p_{1}, and the rest to the right child p2p_{2}, resulting in |𝒪⁡(p1)|=|𝒪⁡(p2)|=4|\mathcal{O}(p_{1})|=|\mathcal{O}(p_{2})|=4. For p1p_{1} and p2p_{2}, the splitting dimension advances to the second attribute, i.e., 𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p1)=𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p2)=2{\mathsf{Dim}}(p_{1})={\mathsf{Dim}}(p_{2})=2, and the split values are set to s⁡(p1)=1.4s(p_{1})=1.4 and s⁡(p2)=5.0s(p_{2})=5.0, respectively. Both splits are balanced, so no dimension is excluded, and all children p3p_{3}–p6p_{6} satisfy |𝒪⁡(p)|≤cl|\mathcal{O}(p)|\leq c_{l} and become leaves.

For each node pp in TT, KHI builds a node-level graph GpG_{p}. Figure 3(b) shows these graphs for M=2M=2: four attached to the leaves p3p_{3}–p6p_{6} (each over two objects), two for p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} (each over four objects), and one for the root p0p_{0} over all objects.

From the above example, we see that under the partitioning strategy of KHI, each leaf-level graph is built over a small subset of objects that are close in the attribute space. For instance, o3o_{3} and o4o_{4}, the closest pair in the attribute space, fall into the same leaf node and are linked as mutual neighbors in Gp4G_{p_{4}}. When neighbor reconstruction is performed for a range predicate BB, the locality of leaf-level graphs in attribute space makes them more likely to contribute in-range neighbors, which can, in many cases, help the reconstructed neighbor lists of visited objects more closely approximate those in the HNSW graph Gh​(OB)G_{h}(O_{B}).

Lemma 0.

The space complexity of KHI is O⁡(n​M⋅log⁡ncl)O(nM\cdot\log\frac{n}{c_{l}}).

Proof. By Lemma 1, the tree TT has height O⁡(log⁡ncl)O(\log\frac{n}{c_{l}}). Since each object belongs to exactly one node at each level of TT, it participates in O⁡(log⁡ncl)O(\log\frac{n}{c_{l}}) node-level filtered HNSW graphs in total. In each single-level filtered HNSW graph, every object stores at most MM neighbors in its adjacency list. Hence, the total space required by all filtered HNSW graphs is O⁡(n​M⋅log⁡ncl)O(nM\cdot\log\frac{n}{c_{l}}). The tree TT contains O⁡(n)O(n) nodes and therefore occupies O⁡(n)O(n) space. Thus, the overall space complexity of KHI is O⁡(n​M⋅log⁡ncl)O(nM\cdot\log\frac{n}{c_{l}}). □\square

4.2. Query Processing

Given an RFANNS query Q=(q,B)Q=(q,B), KHI performs a greedy search over OBO_{B}. Starting from an entry point in OBO_{B}, the search iteratively expands from the current object by aggregating its in-range neighbors from the filtered HNSW graphs.

Entry point selection. With a range predicate BB and an entry-point budget cec_{e} as input, Algorithm 1 constructs a set 𝒫\mathcal{P} of at most cec_{e} entry points for the subsequent greedy search. It performs a depth-first traversal of TT to collect a small set of candidate nodes 𝒞={p}\mathcal{C}=\{p\} such that objects satisfying BB can be efficiently located within their object sets 𝒪⁡(p)\mathcal{O}(p). It then scans 𝒪⁡(p)\mathcal{O}(p) for each tree node p∈𝒞p\in\mathcal{C}, adding at most one object o⊧Bo\models B from each 𝒪⁡(p)\mathcal{O}(p) to 𝒫\mathcal{P}. For notational convenience, any attribute not constrained in BB is treated as having the trivial query range (−∞,+∞)(-\infty,+\infty).

At initialization, the algorithm creates an empty candidate–node set 𝒞\mathcal{C}, an empty entry–point set 𝒫\mathcal{P}, and a stack seeded with the root node prp_{r} and an empty set of covered dimensions (Line 1). In Lines 2–15, the algorithm performs a depth-first traversal over TT while the stack is non-empty and |𝒞|<ce|\mathcal{C}|<c_{e}. In each step, it pops a pair (p,D)(p,D) from the stack (Line 3). Here, for each node pp, the set DD consists of attribute dimensions ai∈Aa_{i}\in A that fall into two categories: (1) dimensions already fully covered by the range predicate, i.e., πi​(ℛ⁡(p))⊆bi\pi_{i}(\mathcal{R}(p))\subseteq b_{i}, where πi​(ℛ​(p))\pi_{i}(\mathcal{R}(p)) denotes the projection of the rectangle ℛ⁡(p)\mathcal{R}(p) onto dimension aia_{i}; and (2) dimensions identified as severely skewed and therefore excluded from further splitting. The algorithm then augments DD with the set of excluded dimensions 𝖡𝖫⁡(p)\mathsf{BL}(p) (Line 4). Intuitively, dimensions in 𝖡𝖫⁡(p)\mathsf{BL}(p) have been identified as highly skewed at pp, so further partitioning along them is discouraged. If all dimensions are covered, i.e., |D|=m|D|=m, the node pp is added to 𝒞\mathcal{C} and its subtree is not explored (Line 5). If pp is a leaf and |D|<m|D|<m, the node is skipped and the traversal continues with the remaining stack entries (Line 6), since not all dimensions in ℛ⁡(p)\mathcal{R}(p) w.r.t. BB are sufficiently refined. Otherwise, the algorithm proceeds to the children of pp.

If 𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p)∈D{\mathsf{Dim}}(p)\in D, then the splitting dimension has already been treated as covered by BB, and no further refinement along 𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p){\mathsf{Dim}}(p) is needed. Consequently, all children of pp are pushed onto the stack with the same set DD (Lines 7–8). If 𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p)∉D{\mathsf{Dim}}(p)\notin D, then for each child pcp_{c} of pp, the algorithm compares the interval [lc,rc]=π𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p)​(ℛ⁡(pc))[l_{c},r_{c}]=\pi_{{\mathsf{Dim}}(p)}(\mathcal{R}(p_{c})) with the range [l𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p),r𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p)][l_{{\mathsf{Dim}}(p)},r_{{\mathsf{Dim}}(p)}] of BB on dimension 𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p){\mathsf{Dim}}(p): If [lc,rc][l_{c},r_{c}] does not intersect [l𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(ni),r𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(ni)][l_{{\mathsf{Dim}}(n_{i})},r_{{\mathsf{Dim}}(n_{i})}], child pcp_{c} is discarded (Line 12). If [lc,rc][l_{c},r_{c}] is fully contained in [l𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(ni),r𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(ni)][l_{{\mathsf{Dim}}(n_{i})},r_{{\mathsf{Dim}}(n_{i})}], then pcp_{c} is pushed with the updated set D∪{𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p)}D\cup\{{\mathsf{Dim}}(p)\} (Lines 13–14); otherwise, pcp_{c} is pushed with the original DD (Lines 15). This depth-first exploration continues until the stack becomes empty or the number of candidate nodes reaches the budget cec_{e}. For each candidate node p∈𝒞p\in\mathcal{C}, the algorithm designates the first object satisfying BB from 𝒪⁡(p)\mathcal{O}(p) as an entry point (Lines 16–18). The resulting set 𝒫⊆OB\mathcal{P}\subseteq O_{B} is well spread over OBO_{B} in the attribute space, providing diverse starting points for the subsequent greedy search and mitigating the risk of being trapped in poor local optima.

On-the-fly neighbor reconstruction. Algorithm 2 reconstructs neighbors of an object oo w.r.t. a range predicate BB. The reconstructed neighbor list 𝒩⁡(o)\mathcal{N}(o) is initialized as empty (Line 1). Starting from the root, it descends the tree; at each level ℓ\ell, it locates the unique node pp such that o∈𝒪⁡(p)o\in\mathcal{O}(p) and scans the neighbors of oo in GpG_{p}. If a neighbor ovo_{v} has already been marked as visited in previous expansions, it is skipped (Line 5); otherwise, ovo_{v} is marked as visited and appended to 𝒩⁡(o)\mathcal{N}(o) if it satisfies BB (Lines 6-8). The procedure terminates once |𝒩⁡(o)|=cn|\mathcal{N}(o)|=c_{n} or the leaf level is reached, and returns the neighbor list 𝒩⁡(o)\mathcal{N}(o).

This reconstruction strategy is deliberately simple: more sophisticated variants would add complexity, and their benefits tend to diminish as the number of attributes mm increases. In contrast, aggregating in-range neighbors along the path of oo provides a direct and effective way to exploit the multi-level structure of KHI.

Query algorithm. Algorithm 3 summarizes the query procedure based on KHI ℐ\mathcal{I}. Given a query Q=(q,B)Q=(q,B) with target size kk, exploration factor ef, entry-point budget cec_{e}, and neighbor budget cnc_{n}, the algorithm maintains two priority queues: a candidate queue 𝒞q\mathcal{C}_{q} and a result queue R^\hat{R} (Line 1). Both queues store pairs (o,δ(o.x,q))(o,\delta(o.x,q)), ordered by distance to qq; 𝒞q\mathcal{C}_{q} is a min-heap, whereas R^\hat{R} is a bounded max-heap of capacity ef.

The algorithm first invokes Algorithm 1 to obtain a set 𝒫\mathcal{P} of entry points in OBO_{B} (Line 2). For each o∈𝒫o\in\mathcal{P}, it computes δ(o.x,q)\delta(o.x,q), inserts (o,dist)(o,\textit{dist}) into both R^\hat{R} and 𝒞q\mathcal{C}_{q}, and marks oo as visited (Lines 3–6). While 𝒞q\mathcal{C}_{q} is non-empty and either |R^|<ef|\hat{R}|<\textit{ef} or the best candidate in 𝒞q\mathcal{C}_{q} is no farther than the worst object in R^\hat{R}, the algorithm extracts from 𝒞q\mathcal{C}_{q} the current closest object ouo_{u} (Line 8). Its neighbors 𝒩⁡(ou)\mathcal{N}(o_{u}) under BB are reconstructed by Algorithm 2 (Line 9). For each ov∈𝒩⁡(ou)o_{v}\in\mathcal{N}(o_{u}), the distance δ(ov.x,q)\delta(o_{v}.x,q) is computed and (ov,dist)(o_{v},\textit{dist}) is inserted into both R^\hat{R} and 𝒞q\mathcal{C}_{q} (Lines 10–12). If |R^||\hat{R}| exceeds ef, the farthest object in R^\hat{R} is removed to keep the result queue bounded (Line 13). After the greedy search terminates, the kk closest objects in R^\hat{R} are returned as the query result to QQ (Line 14).

In our implementation, we set ce=kc_{e}=k, since larger values bring only limited gains in search quality. The neighbor budget is set to cn=Mc_{n}=M, matching the maximum degree bound in the filtered HNSW graphs for the same reason.

4.3. Index Construction

Considering the structure of KHI, index construction proceeds as follows. First, we build the partitioning tree TT over all objects in the attribute space. Then, leveraging the hierarchy of TT, we construct a single-level filtered HNSW graph at each node to capture proximity relationships among the corresponding embeddings.

Partitioning tree construction. We construct the partitioning tree TT in a top-down manner, as shown in Algorithm 4. Starting from the root node prp_{r}, each node pp stores a splitting dimension 𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p){\mathsf{Dim}}(p) and a set of excluded dimensions 𝖡𝖫⁡(p)⊆{1,…,m}\mathsf{BL}(p)\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}. The construction proceeds through a stack-based traversal.

When a node pp is popped from the stack, partitioning stops if |𝒪⁡(p)|≤cl|\mathcal{O}(p)|\leq c_{l} or all mm dimensions have been included in 𝖡𝖫⁡(p)\mathsf{BL}(p) (Line 6). Otherwise, we advance 𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p){\mathsf{Dim}}(p) in a round-robin manner until we find an eligible (non-excluded) dimension (Lines 7-8), and then determine the split value s⁡(p)s(p) on dimension 𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p){\mathsf{Dim}}(p) (Lines 9-10). Concretely, let {o.t.t𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p)∣o∈𝒪(p)}\{o.t.t_{{\mathsf{Dim}}(p)}\mid o\in\mathcal{O}(p)\} be the multiset of attribute values on this dimension, sorted in ascending order. We define 𝗆𝗂𝖽=⌊(|𝒪⁡(p)|−1)/2⌋\mathsf{mid}=\lfloor(|\mathcal{O}(p)|-1)/2\rfloor and choose s⁡(p)s(p) as the value at position 𝗆𝗂𝖽\mathsf{mid}, which induces two subsets 𝒪⁡(pl)\mathcal{O}(p_{l}) and 𝒪⁡(pr)\mathcal{O}(p_{r}) for the left and right child, respectively (Lines 11–12). We then check the balance condition. If τ⋅min⁡(|𝒪⁡(pl)|,|𝒪⁡(pr)|)≤max⁡(|𝒪⁡(pl)|,|𝒪⁡(pr)|)\tau\cdot\min(|\mathcal{O}(p_{l})|,|\mathcal{O}(p_{r})|)\leq\max(|\mathcal{O}(p_{l})|,|\mathcal{O}(p_{r})|), the split is considered skewed: 𝖣𝗂𝗆⁡(p){\mathsf{Dim}}(p) is added to 𝖡𝖫⁡(p)\mathsf{BL}(p) and pp is pushed back onto the stack to retry with another dimension (Lines 14–15). Otherwise, we accept the split, create the two children, assign to each the next splitting dimension in the round-robin order, inherit the set of excluded dimensions, and push them onto the stack to continue partitioning (Lines 17–20).

Filtered HNSW graph construction. Given the partitioning tree TT, we construct for each node pp a single-level filtered HNSW graph GpG_{p} in a bottom-up manner (Algorithm 5). We first build a queue of tree nodes ordered from leaves to root: nodes are grouped by depth, and the levels are enqueued from the deepest level up to the root, ensuring that every child is processed before its parent (Line 1).

If the dequeued node pp is a leaf, we build GpG_{p} by invoking the standard HNSW building procedure with maximum degree bound MM (Lines 4–5). Otherwise, we set GpG_{p} to GplG_{p_{l}} (Line 8), and then incrementally merge the objects in 𝒪⁡(pr)\mathcal{O}(p_{r}) into GpG_{p}. For each object o∈𝒪⁡(pr)o\in\mathcal{O}(p_{r}), we run a greedy search on the current GpG_{p} to obtain a candidate set R^\hat{R} of up to efb\textit{ef}_{b} objects (Line 10). Its neighbor list in GpG_{p} is then determined by applying the RNG-based heuristic from Section 2.2 to the union of candidates from the parent and right-child graphs, obtaining an MM-bounded neighbor list while retaining high-quality neighbors (Line 11). Finally, we update neighbor lists of affected objects in 𝒪⁡(pl)\mathcal{O}(p_{l}): for each o^∈𝒪⁡(pl)∩𝒩⁡(o)\hat{o}\in\mathcal{O}(p_{l})\cap\mathcal{N}(o) in GpG_{p}, we refine 𝒩⁡(o^)\mathcal{N}(\hat{o}) in GpG_{p} by applying the same RNG-based pruning to o∪𝒩⁡(o^){o}\cup\mathcal{N}(\hat{o}) in GpG_{p} (Lines 12–13). Processing all nodes in this bottom-up order yields the collection {Gp}\{G_{p}\} of graphs attached to the nodes of KHI (Line 14). In our implementation, we set efb=M\textit{ef}_{b}=M.

Parallel graph construction. In the overall index construction, building the filtered HNSW graphs dominates the runtime because it requires many distance computations between high-dimensional embeddings (see (Yu et al., 2025) for details). To reduce construction time, we parallelize graph construction while keeping the resulting graphs identical to the sequential version.

Recall that the nodes of TT are grouped by depth in a bottom-up order. Since the construction of graph GpG_{p} at a node pp only depends on the graphs of its children, all nodes on the same level can be processed independently, so we first build graphs in a level-wise parallel fashion. However, near the upper levels of the tree, the number of nodes per level becomes small and the workload across nodes can become imbalanced, limiting the benefit of purely level-wise parallelization. To address this, we introduce a threshold τp\tau_{p} on the number of nodes per level: when a level contains fewer than τp\tau_{p} nodes, we switch from level-wise parallelism to intra-node parallelism. In this case, each remaining node pp typically has a large 𝒪⁡(pr)\mathcal{O}(p_{r}), and we parallelize the merge step for objects in 𝒪⁡(pr)\mathcal{O}(p_{r}) (Lines 9–13 of Algorithm 5) by distributing these objects across worker threads, each independently running the greedy search and RNG-based pruning to update the corresponding neighbor lists in GpG_{p}. In our implementation, we set τp=100\tau_{p}=100.

Discussion. Our partitioning tree TT is inspired by classical KD-trees but departs from standard variants in several key aspects. Each node maintains a set of excluded dimensions 𝖡𝖫⁡(p)\mathsf{BL}(p) and uses a balance threshold τ\tau to avoid highly skewed splits, which yields a provable bound on the tree height. Moreover, TT is tailored to RFANNS: it is built purely in the attribute space, and its nodes serve as anchors for filtered HNSW graphs rather than for traditional point-location queries as in standard KD-trees. These design choices are driven by the requirements of RFANNS and, to the best of our knowledge, have not been explored in existing KD-tree–based indexes.

5. Experiments

5.1. Experimental Setup

Our experimental evaluation focuses on two aspects: query performance and index efficiency. For query performance, we compare our method against baselines under various query settings. For index efficiency, we report the index construction time and the empirical space usage of our method and baselines.

Datasets. To evaluate the performance of all methods, we use four real-world public datasets. Since few public corpora provide both multi-attribute numeric metadata and corresponding vector representations, we construct our evaluation datasets by encoding the raw content with open-source embedding models and pairing the resulting vectors with the original attributes. The resulting datasets are summarized in Table 1. 𝖫𝖺𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{Laion} 11 1 https://laion.ai/blog/laion-400-open-dataset/ contains image–text pairs with three numeric attributes: image width, image height, and a similarity score. 𝖬𝖲𝖬𝖺𝗋𝖼𝗈\mathsf{MSMarco} 22 2 https://microsoft.github.io/msmarco/ and 𝖣𝖡𝖫𝖯\mathsf{DBLP} 33 3 https://open.aminer.cn/open/article?id=655db2202ab17a072284bc0c are text collections with document-level statistics such as the number of words, sentences, and citations. 𝖸𝗈𝗎𝗍𝗎𝖻𝖾\mathsf{Youtube} 44 4 https://research.google.com/youtube8m/ consists of video records with temporal and popularity metadata, including publication year, the number of views, and the number of likes.

Algorithms. Among existing RFANNS indexes, we consider two representative methods, SeRF and iRangeGraph, as introduced in Section 2.3. SeRF is designed for single-attribute range filters. Although its paper outlines a possible extension to multi-attribute RFANNS, this variant is only described at a high level and, to the best of our knowledge, has not been implemented. Since our focus is on multi-attribute RFANNS, we do not evaluate SeRF experimentally and instead use iRangeGraph as the main RFANNS baseline.

In addition to iRangeGraph, we also include a simple pre-filtering baseline. Given a query Q=(q,B)Q=(q,B), 𝖯𝗋𝖾𝖿𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{Prefiltering} first scans all objects to materialize the subset OBO_{B}. It then performs exact nearest neighbor search for qq over OBO_{B} in the embedding space by exhaustively computing distances and returning the kk closest objects.

Queries. For each dataset, we generate 1,0001{,}000 RFANNS queries of the form Q=(q,B)Q=(q,B). During dataset construction, we randomly sample 1,0001{,}000 raw objects from the original corpus and encode them with the same embedding model used to build the dataset; these vectors are stored separately and used only as query embeddings.

The range predicate BB is generated in the attribute space with a target selectivity σ\sigma and a relative tolerance parameter 𝗍𝗈𝗅\mathsf{tol}. Following iRangeGraph, we parameterize the target selectivity as σ=1/2i\sigma=1/2^{i}. Since multi-attribute range predicates often result in relatively small selectivities in practice, we focus on i∈{4,6,8}i\in\{4,6,8\}, i.e., σ∈{1/16,1/64,1/256}\sigma\in\{1/16,1/64,1/256\}.

To instantiate BB, we first draw a random sample of attribute tuples and, for each attribute, build a sorted list of finite values to support quantile queries. For each query, we derive per-attribute intervals by selecting lower and upper quantiles on the sampled tuples so that the empirical selectivity of the resulting BB lies within [σ⁡(1−𝗍𝗈𝗅),σ⁡(1+𝗍𝗈𝗅)][\sigma(1-\mathsf{tol}),\,\sigma(1+\mathsf{tol})]. By default, we set 𝗍𝗈𝗅=0.5\mathsf{tol}=0.5.

Equipment. All algorithms are implemented in C++, compiled with the g++ compiler at -O3 optimization level, and run on a Linux machine equipped with an Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPU @ 2.10 GHz and 256 GB of RAM.

5.2. Query performance

Overall performance. We evaluate query efficiency using queries per second (QPS), defined as the number of RFANNS queries processed per second, and report the trade-off between recall and QPS. Figure 4 summarizes the query performance of the three methods on all four datasets. For each figure, the curve is obtained by varying the exploration factor ef on a fixed index, yielding a series of points with different recall–QPS combinations. Both KHI and iRangeGraph use a maximum degree bound M=32M=32. In this experiment, we set the cardinality of BB to mm (i.e., each range predicate constrains all attributes) and fix the target size k=10k=10. We make the following observations:

(1) The two graph-based methods, KHI and iRangeGraph, achieve high recall across all datasets and selectivities: on 𝖫𝖺𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{Laion}, 𝖬𝖲𝖬𝖺𝗋𝖼𝗈\mathsf{MSMarco}, and 𝖣𝖡𝖫𝖯\mathsf{DBLP} the recall exceeds 0.990.99, and on the more challenging 𝖸𝗈𝗎𝗍𝗎𝖻𝖾\mathsf{Youtube} it remains above 0.90.9. However, their query throughput shows clear differences.

(2) When σ∈{1/16,1/64,1/256}\sigma\in\{1/16,1/64,1/256\}, KHI consistently outperforms iRangeGraph in QPS at comparable recall levels. At recall 0.950.95, the QPS gains on 𝖫𝖺𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{Laion} are 1.66×1.66\times, 2.34×2.34\times, and 3.99×3.99\times over iRangeGraph as σ\sigma decreases from 1/161/16 to 1/2561/256; on 𝖬𝖲𝖬𝖺𝗋𝖼𝗈\mathsf{MSMarco}, the corresponding speedups are 1.20×1.20\times, 1.67×1.67\times, and 4.92×4.92\times; and on 𝖣𝖡𝖫𝖯\mathsf{DBLP}, they are 1.76×1.76\times, 1.48×1.48\times, and 3.15×3.15\times, respectively. On the more challenging 𝖸𝗈𝗎𝗍𝗎𝖻𝖾\mathsf{Youtube} dataset, KHI yields 1.68×1.68\times, 8.89×8.89\times, and 38.08×38.08\times speedups at recall 0.90.9 for σ=1/16\sigma=1/16, 1/641/64, and 1/2561/256, respectively. Averaged over 𝖫𝖺𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{Laion}, 𝖬𝖲𝖬𝖺𝗋𝖼𝗈\mathsf{MSMarco}, and 𝖣𝖡𝖫𝖯\mathsf{DBLP} and the three selectivities, KHI attains an overall speedup of 2.46×2.46\times in QPS compared with iRangeGraph, while on 𝖸𝗈𝗎𝗍𝗎𝖻𝖾\mathsf{Youtube} the average speedup reaches 16.22×16.22\times. Overall, the advantage grows more pronounced for lower selectivities and more challenging datasets.

(3) When the target recall is relaxed below 1.01.0, both KHI and iRangeGraph yield notable speedups over 𝖯𝗋𝖾𝖿𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{Prefiltering}. At recall 0.950.95 on 𝖫𝖺𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{Laion}, 𝖬𝖲𝖬𝖺𝗋𝖼𝗈\mathsf{MSMarco}, and 𝖣𝖡𝖫𝖯\mathsf{DBLP} (and 0.90.9 on 𝖸𝗈𝗎𝗍𝗎𝖻𝖾\mathsf{Youtube}), KHI consistently achieves higher QPS than 𝖯𝗋𝖾𝖿𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{Prefiltering} on all datasets, with an average speedup of 35.59×35.59\times. In the same setting, iRangeGraph also outperforms 𝖯𝗋𝖾𝖿𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{Prefiltering} on all datasets except 𝖸𝗈𝗎𝗍𝗎𝖻𝖾\mathsf{Youtube}, with an average speedup of 24.91×24.91\times; on 𝖸𝗈𝗎𝗍𝗎𝖻𝖾\mathsf{Youtube}, however, iRangeGraph falls short of 𝖯𝗋𝖾𝖿𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{Prefiltering}, as shown in Figure 4(e) and Figure 4(i).

Convergence of the distance threshold. To better understand how the graph-based methods behave, we further examine the evolution of the distance threshold during greedy search. We measure the search progress in 𝗁𝗈𝗉𝗌{\mathsf{hops}}, where one hop corresponds to expanding the neighbors of a candidate object. At a given hop, we define the distance threshold as the distance from qq to the farthest object in R^\hat{R}, where R^\hat{R} denotes the current set of best-so-far candidates. In this experiment, we use the same settings as in the overall query performance study. We report the evolution of the distance threshold at ef=300\textit{ef}=300 for σ∈{1/16,1/64,1/256}\sigma\in\{1/16,1/64,1/256\}.

Figure 5 shows how this threshold evolves with the number of hops across all datasets and selectivities. For KHI, across all datasets and selectivities, the distance threshold decreases rapidly in the first few hops and then quickly stabilizes. This suggests that KHI is able to tighten the distance threshold more aggressively and prune inferior candidates earlier, while still preserving high recall. In contrast, for iRangeGraph, the distance threshold decays much more slowly and often remains high over many hops, especially for smaller selectivities, e.g., σ=1/64\sigma=1/64 and σ=1/256\sigma=1/256. As discussed in Section 3.1, this behavior stems from its reliance on many out-of-range neighbors. Thus, iRangeGraph tends to explore more candidates during search. These search dynamics are consistent with the higher QPS achieved by KHI, compared with iRangeGraph at comparable recall levels in Figure 4.

Varying target size kk. We study the impact of the target size kk on query performance and present the results on 𝖫𝖺𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{Laion} as a representative example. We fix the target recall at 0.950.95 and evaluate QPS while varying kk from 2020 to 100100, as shown in Figure 6; the case k=10k=10 has already been reported in Figure 4. All other settings follow the overall query performance study.

We fix the target recall at 0.950.95 and report the QPS achieved by KHI and iRangeGraph on 𝖫𝖺𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{Laion} while varying k∈{10,20,50,100}k\in\{10,20,50,100\}. When σ=1/16\sigma=1/16, KHI achieves speedups over iRangeGraph, with QPS improvements of 1.66×1.66\times, 1.91×1.91\times, 2.38×2.38\times, and 2.60×2.60\times at k=10k=10, 2020, 5050, and 100100, respectively. For σ=1/64\sigma=1/64, the gains become larger, with speedups of about 2.34×2.34\times, 2.51×2.51\times, 4.81×4.81\times, and 5.10×5.10\times for k=10k=10, 2020, 5050, and 100100, respectively. For the case σ=1/256\sigma=1/256, the advantage of KHI is even more pronounced, reaching 3.99×3.99\times, 4.90×4.90\times, 7.20×7.20\times, and 10.52×10.52\times for k=10k=10, 2020, 5050, and 100100, respectively. Overall, the performance gap between KHI and iRangeGraph widens as kk increases, especially under low selectivity. This effect may be attributed to the fact that larger kk forces the search to explore a broader local neighborhood; in this regime, KHI benefits from higher-quality in-range neighbors, whereas iRangeGraph spends more hops on out-of-range candidates, so KHI can obtain the kk nearest neighbors with fewer expansions and consequently higher QPS. We also observe that, when the recall is relaxed to 0.950.95, both KHI and iRangeGraph achieve substantially higher QPS than 𝖯𝗋𝖾𝖿𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{Prefiltering}. On 𝖫𝖺𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{Laion}, averaging over k∈{10,20,50,100}k\in\{10,20,50,100\}, their QPS speedups over 𝖯𝗋𝖾𝖿𝗂𝗅\mathsf{Prefil}-𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{tering} are 62.76×62.76\times and 24.16×24.16\times, respectively.

Varying cardinality of BB. We study the effect of the cardinality of BB on query performance. We report the results on 𝖣𝖡𝖫𝖯\mathsf{DBLP}; the other datasets exhibit similar trends. We fix the target recall at 0.950.95 and evaluate QPS while varying the cardinality of BB from 22 to 44. All other settings follow the overall query performance study. When the cardinality of BB is less than mm, for each query we choose the constrained attributes uniformly at random from the mm attributes. In Figure 7, we plot the cases where the cardinality of BB is 22 and 33; the case where the cardinality of BB equals mm has already been reported in Figure 4 and is omitted here for brevity.

When σ=1/16\sigma=1/16, KHI achieves about 1.06×1.06\times, 1.29×1.29\times, and 1.76×1.76\times higher QPS than iRangeGraph when the cardinality of BB is 22, 33, and 44, respectively. For σ=1/64\sigma=1/64, the speedup ranges from roughly parity when the cardinality of BB is 22 to about 1.43×1.43\times and 1.48×1.48\times when it is 33 and 44. For σ=1/256\sigma=1/256, the gains become more pronounced, reaching around 1.53×1.53\times, 2.47×2.47\times, and 3.15×3.15\times for cardinalities 22, 33, and 44, respectively. These results indicate that, as BB involves more attributes, KHI increasingly outperforms iRangeGraph, especially under low selectivity, highlighting the benefit of its attribute-space partitioning and and the resulting high-quality graphs. Moreover, compared with the exhaustive 𝖯𝗋𝖾𝖿𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{Prefiltering} baseline on 𝖣𝖡𝖫𝖯\mathsf{DBLP}, KHI and iRangeGraph achieve average QPS speedups of 39.46×39.46\times and 27.81×27.81\times, respectively, across these settings.

5.3. Index construction

Index construction time. Since single-threaded index construction runs slow on our datasets, we report multi-threaded construction times under a 16-thread configuration with maximum degree bound M=32M=32 for both KHI and iRangeGraph. As shown in Table 2, across the four datasets, KHI can be built in about 2,0002{,}000–5,5005{,}500 s, whereas iRangeGraph requires roughly 6,7006{,}700–17,80017{,}800 s. These correspond to speedups of 3.35×3.35\times, 3.01×3.01\times, 3.24×3.24\times, and 3.49×3.49\times, respectively, i.e., an average reduction of construction time by about a factor of 3.273.27. This confirms that our parallelization strategy, which combines level-wise and intra-node parallelism, substantially accelerates index construction compared with the pure level-wise parallelism used in iRangeGraph.

Index size. Table 3 reports the index sizes on all datasets, with M=32M=32 for both indexes. Overall, the two indexes occupy comparable space: across all datasets, the size of KHI differs from that of iRangeGraph by less than 15%15\%. Although our partitioning tree TT is not strictly balanced, the skew-aware splitting strategy keeps most objects at moderate depths, so that only a small fraction reside in deeper levels. As a result, the additional nodes and their filtered HNSW graphs incur only limited extra space. Further details on the empirical tree height are provided in (Yu et al., 2025).

6. Related Work

Approximate nearest neighbor search. Approximate nearest neighbor search in high-dimensional Euclidean spaces has been extensively studied. Existing methods can be broadly categorized into graph-based (Malkov et al., 2014; Harwood and Drummond, 2016; Malkov and Yashunin, 2018; Li et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2019; Jayaram Subramanya et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2025a), quantization-based (Jegou et al., 2010; Babenko and Lempitsky, 2014a; Babenko and Lempitsky, 2014b; André et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2020; Gao and Long, 2024), and hashing-based (Datar et al., 2004; Tao et al., 2010; Gan et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2015); we refer readers to recent tutorials (Echihabi et al., 2021; Qin et al., 2021), surveys (Li et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021b; Wang et al., 2023b), and benchmark studies (Aumüller et al., 2020; Aumüller and Ceccarello, 2023) for a comprehensive overview of this literature. Among these categories, graph-based methods have demonstrated particularly strong performance: HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, 2018), NSG (Fu et al., 2019), and DiskANN (Jayaram Subramanya et al., 2019) have been widely adopted in industry (Wang et al., 2021a). More recently, several GPU-accelerated graph-based ANN methods (Zhao et al., 2020; Groh et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022; Ootomo et al., 2024) have been proposed to increase throughput by exploiting massive parallelism. These methods are highly optimized for ANN without attribute constraints. In contrast, we focus on extending ANN to handle multi-attribute range filters efficiently, a setting not addressed in the above line of work.

Range-filtering nearest neighbor search. Motivated by the practical importance of attribute-filtered ANN queries, many algorithms and systems have been proposed (Cai et al., 2024; Engels et al., 2024; Gollapudi et al., 2023; Mohoney et al., 2023; Patel et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023a; Wei et al., 2020; Zuo et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2021a). We refer readers to the survey (Lin et al., 2025) for a comprehensive overview. Across different application scenarios, attribute predicates can be broadly grouped into equality predicates, numeric range predicates, and more general comparison predicates. For equality predicates (Cai et al., 2024; Gollapudi et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a), objects carry categorical labels and the goal is to retrieve the kk nearest neighbors whose labels exactly match the query label(s). This setting differs from ours, where queries impose multi-dimensional numeric constraints. Range predicates enforce lower and/or upper bounds on numeric attributes. Most existing RFANNS methods for range predicates focus on single-attribute filters (Engels et al., 2024; Zuo et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024), where the condition is specified on a single numeric dimension. In contrast, we study RFANNS with multi-attribute numeric ranges, filling this gap. For general comparison predicates, several systems support attribute-filtered ANN queries over heterogeneous attributes, including numeric, categorical, and other application-specific fields (Mohoney et al., 2023; Patel et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2021a; Wei et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2025b). Prior work has shown that different attribute types exhibit markedly different properties and that strong performance typically requires index designs tailored to a specific predicate class (Xu et al., 2024). Since our method is specifically designed for numeric range predicates, we therefore compare primarily against specialized RFANNS indexes rather than these general-purpose systems. In addition, GPU-based methods for attribute-filtered ANN queries have recently been explored (Xi et al., 2025); these techniques are largely orthogonal to our contribution and could in principle be combined with our index.

Dynamic range-filtering nearest neighbor search. Several wo-rks (Jiang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2025) have been proposed to support RFANNS in dynamic settings. DIGRA (Jiang et al., 2025) organizes objects in a B-tree over attributes and maintains HNSW graphs at tree nodes, both of which admit efficient maintenance under insertions and deletions. DSG (Peng et al., 2025) proposes a dynamic segment graph structure, while requiring only O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) new edges in expectation per insertion.

7. Conclusion

In this paper, we study RFANNS in high-dimensional Euclidean spaces with multi-attribute numeric range predicates, a setting that is increasingly important in modern vector databases but has been insufficiently explored by existing work. We propose KHI, a tailored RFANNS index that combines an attribute-space partitioning tree with filtered HNSW graphs anchored at tree nodes. The partitioning tree employs a skew-aware splitting strategy, which adapts to attribute distributions while still admitting provable bounds on the tree height. On top of this structure, we design an efficient query algorithm that relies only on in-range neighbors yet still achieves high recall and strong query performance.

We conduct extensive experiments on four real-world datasets and compare KHI with iRangeGraph and a prefiltering baseline. The results demonstrate that KHI consistently achieves better query throughput than the baselines. Specifically, KHI achieves an average QPS speedup of 2.46×2.46\times over iRangeGraph on 𝖫𝖺𝗂𝗈𝗇\mathsf{Laion}, 𝖣𝖡𝖫𝖯\mathsf{DBLP}, and 𝖬𝖲𝖬𝖺𝗋𝖼𝗈\mathsf{MSMarco}, and 16.22×16.22\times on the more challenging 𝖸𝗈𝗎𝗍𝗎𝖻𝖾\mathsf{Youtube}, with gains further increasing for smaller selectivities, larger kk, and higher predicate cardinality. When the recall is relaxed to 0.950.95 (or 0.90.9 on 𝖸𝗈𝗎𝗍𝗎𝖻𝖾\mathsf{Youtube}), KHI also consistently outperforms 𝖯𝗋𝖾𝖿𝗂𝗅𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathsf{Prefiltering} in QPS across all datasets, with an average speedup of 35.59×35.59\times. In terms of index construction, KHI is on average 3.27×3.27\times faster than iRangeGraph under a 16-thread configuration, while incurring at most roughly a 15%15\% space overhead compared with iRangeGraph. Future work includes supporting fully dynamic workloads and exploring GPU implementations for large-scale deployments.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
